questions.topic: Transport versus handling of an ordinary Schedule II drug
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist needs help moving and counting oxycodone tablets. Both a licensed noncertified pharmacy technician and a licensed certified pharmacy technician are available. The pharmacist has approved the relevant tasks under the pharmacy's written procedures and will supervise them. Which assignments are permitted? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Ordinary technician may assist transport; certified technician may assist transport and handling under supervision and documented approval.
questions.critical_exception: Certification and the nature of the task matter; this is not the special non-abuse-deterrent hydrocodone-only rule.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Without certification, assign transport rather than counting.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist needs help moving and counting oxycodone tablets. Both a licensed noncertified pharmacy technician and a licensed certified pharmacy technician are available. The pharmacist has approved the relevant tasks under the pharmacy's written procedures and will supervise them. Which assignments are permitted? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Have the noncertified technician assist with transport.
choices.why: Correct. Section 8.05(2)(a) expressly allows supervised, approved transport.

choices.text: Have the noncertified technician count oxycodone tablets.
choices.why: Incorrect. Handling is not authorized for the noncertified technician under this provision.

choices.text: Have the certified technician count oxycodone tablets.
choices.why: Correct. Approved supervised handling of ordinary Schedule II products is within certified technician scope.

choices.text: Transfer responsibility for Schedule II security entirely to the certified technician.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacist retains direct responsibility.

choices.text: Permit the certified technician to perform these tasks without pharmacist supervision.
choices.why: Incorrect. The authorization requires supervision.

questions.topic: Checked refill that still requires pharmacist consultation during break
questions.trigger: The sole pharmacist is taking a permitted on-premises meal break. A patient arrives for a refill that the pharmacist already checked, but the pharmacist specifically determined that a consultation must occur before release. A technician offers to release it and have the pharmacist call afterward. What is appropriate?
questions.legal_decision: Hold this refill until the required pharmacist consultation occurs.
questions.critical_exception: A checked refill is eligible for release during a temporary absence only if the pharmacist determined consultation was unnecessary.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If checked and determined not to require consultation, a refill may be released during the permitted absence.
questions.stem: The sole pharmacist is taking a permitted on-premises meal break. A patient arrives for a refill that the pharmacist already checked, but the pharmacist specifically determined that a consultation must occur before release. A technician offers to release it and have the pharmacist call afterward. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Release under the special logged new-prescription procedure.
choices.why: Incorrect. This is a refill requiring consultation, not an eligible new prescription.

choices.text: Release because all checked refills qualify.
choices.why: Incorrect. The no-consultation condition is not met.

choices.text: Release if a technician documents an intended callback.
choices.why: Incorrect. Documentation does not substitute for the required pre-release consultation.

choices.text: Release if the patient has taken the medicine before.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prior use does not override the pharmacist's determination.

choices.text: Hold the refill until the pharmacist can provide the required consultation.
choices.why: Correct. Both conditions must be met for release during the absence.

critical_error_options.reason: Releases a refill despite expressly required consultation.

questions.topic: Institutional director's personnel documentation duties
questions.trigger: A hospital pharmacy uses certified technicians, noncertified technicians and trainees. A Board inspector requests documentation about those employees and their assigned roles. Which records must the institutional pharmacy director make available on request? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Provide current employed technician/trainee list, written delegated duties and written scopes of responsibility.
questions.critical_exception: The obligation is not limited to staff who are nationally certified.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An oral explanation is not a substitute for the required written descriptions.
questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy uses certified technicians, noncertified technicians and trainees. A Board inspector requests documentation about those employees and their assigned roles. Which records must the institutional pharmacy director make available on request? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A list of currently employed certified technicians, technicians and trainees.
choices.why: Correct. This is required by subsection (a).

choices.text: Written descriptions of the scopes of responsibility.
choices.why: Correct. This is required by subsection (c).

choices.text: Every employee's private bank statement.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cited rule does not require this.

choices.text: A written description of the delegated duties.
choices.why: Correct. This is required by subsection (b).

choices.text: Only a list of certified technicians, excluding trainees.
choices.why: Incorrect. The required list encompasses all three categories.

questions.topic: On-duty pharmacist access to records when MOR absent
questions.trigger: An investigator of the Massachusetts Board requests pharmacy records during normal operating hours. The manager of record is off site. The on-duty pharmacist says that only the manager has permission to access the files. Which conclusion best describes the on-duty pharmacist's responsibility?
questions.legal_decision: On-duty pharmacist must have access to all pharmacy records and be able to provide requested records to Board investigators.
questions.critical_exception: The manager's absence does not transfer away the on-duty duty.
questions.counterfactual_flip: The on-duty pharmacist can comply when authorized access and retrieval are available.
questions.stem: An investigator of the Massachusetts Board requests pharmacy records during normal operating hours. The manager of record is off site. The on-duty pharmacist says that only the manager has permission to access the files. Which conclusion best describes the on-duty pharmacist's responsibility?

choices.text: Only the manager must be able to retrieve records.
choices.why: Incorrect. The duty also applies to the on-duty pharmacist.

choices.text: The pharmacist must have access and be able to provide the requested pharmacy records.
choices.why: Correct. This is an express on-duty responsibility.

choices.text: The pharmacist may permanently defer all requests until the manager returns.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule requires ability to provide requested records while on duty.

choices.text: A technician's ability to access records eliminates the pharmacist's duty.
choices.why: Incorrect. Delegation does not remove the pharmacist's responsibility.

choices.text: The duty only applies to Schedule II records.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule refers to all pharmacy records.

questions.topic: Personal registration renewal within 60 days after expiration
questions.trigger: A pharmacist's Massachusetts personal registration expired December 31 of an even-numbered year. Forty-five days later the pharmacist discovers the lapse. There is no military extension, suspension, revocation or other special circumstance. Which statements are correct under 247 CMR 4.02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Renew using applicable fees including late fee; no practice while expired; the specific more-than-60-day and more-than-two-year conditions are not triggered solely by this lapse.
questions.critical_exception: Short expiration is not permission to practice.
questions.counterfactual_flip: After more than 60 days additional Board conditions may apply; after more than two years MPJE is required.
questions.stem: A pharmacist's Massachusetts personal registration expired December 31 of an even-numbered year. Forty-five days later the pharmacist discovers the lapse. There is no military extension, suspension, revocation or other special circumstance. Which statements are correct under 247 CMR 4.02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: This 45-day lapse alone triggers mandatory MPJE retesting.
choices.why: Incorrect. The nondisciplinary lapse threshold for that requirement is more than two years.

choices.text: This 45-day lapse alone triggers the more-than-60-day provision.
choices.why: Incorrect. That threshold has not been crossed.

choices.text: The pharmacist may practice during the first 60 days after expiration.
choices.why: Incorrect. Any practice after expiration is unlicensed absent a special exception.

choices.text: Applicable renewal, back-license and late fees are required for late renewal.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (2) provides for those fees.

choices.text: The pharmacist must refrain from practice until registration is renewed.
choices.why: Correct. The lapse is not a grace period for practice.

critical_error_options.reason: Treats an expired registration as authorization to practice.

questions.topic: Reporting loss of national technician certification
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy employs a licensed certified technician whose national certification has been revoked. The technician's Massachusetts pharmacy technician license remains active. Which reporting obligation applies specifically to the loss of certification?
questions.legal_decision: Both pharmacy and individual licensee must report loss of certification within 14 calendar days.
questions.critical_exception: State licensure remaining active does not eliminate certification-loss reporting.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no loss of certification or other reportable event occurred this particular reporting rule would not trigger.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy employs a licensed certified technician whose national certification has been revoked. The technician's Massachusetts pharmacy technician license remains active. Which reporting obligation applies specifically to the loss of certification?

choices.text: The technician and the pharmacy must report within 14 calendar days.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (4) applies to each pharmacy and individual licensed by the Board.

choices.text: No report is required because the technician license is still active.
choices.why: Incorrect. Loss of certification is separately reportable.

choices.text: Only the pharmacy must report and the technician need not report.
choices.why: Incorrect. Both licensees have a duty.

choices.text: Only the national certifying body must report.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Massachusetts rule imposes duties on licensees.

choices.text: The technician reports only at the next renewal.
choices.why: Incorrect. The deadline is 14 calendar days.

questions.topic: Out-of-state Schedule II nonnarcotic prescription presented after five-day window
questions.trigger: A prescriber who is licensed and DEA-registered in Illinois, but not authorized to prescribe in Massachusetts, issues a methylphenidate prescription on November 4. A Massachusetts retail pharmacist receives it on November 11 and verifies its authenticity. No special exception applies. Which statement is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Do not fill under the out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II pathway when issued more than five days earlier.
questions.critical_exception: The ordinary 30-day Massachusetts Schedule II rule does not extend this specific interstate authorization.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If received within the five-day window and verified, the interstate pathway could apply.
questions.stem: A prescriber who is licensed and DEA-registered in Illinois, but not authorized to prescribe in Massachusetts, issues a methylphenidate prescription on November 4. A Massachusetts retail pharmacist receives it on November 11 and verifies its authenticity. No special exception applies. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Fill because methylphenidate is not a narcotic.
choices.why: Incorrect. Nonnarcotic status permits the interstate pathway but does not eliminate its five-day limit.

choices.text: Fill because verification replaces the time limit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification and timeliness are separate conditions.

choices.text: Do not fill this prescription; obtain a new lawful prescription if appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Seven days have elapsed, beyond the special five-day authorization.

choices.text: Fill because all Schedule II prescriptions are valid for 30 days regardless of origin.
choices.why: Incorrect. The specific interstate rule is more restrictive.

choices.text: Fill only half now and the remainder later to satisfy the time rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. A partial fill does not restore authority to fill the original prescription.

critical_error_options.reason: Nonnarcotic status permits the interstate pathway but does not eliminate its five-day limit.

questions.topic: Out-of-state oral Schedule IV prescription and follow-up request
questions.trigger: A Vermont practitioner authorized there and federally registered sends an otherwise lawful oral Schedule IV prescription to a Massachusetts pharmacist. Assume a valid electronic-prescribing exception applies and the prescription was issued today. Which actions are required under the Massachusetts out-of-state prescription rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Verify authenticity/validity and record the request for a written follow-up within seven days or shorter federal limit.
questions.critical_exception: An authorized oral transmission and successful verification do not waive the special follow-up request.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the order were from a Massachusetts-authorized practitioner, §18(c)'s interstate-specific provision would not govern.
questions.stem: A Vermont practitioner authorized there and federally registered sends an otherwise lawful oral Schedule IV prescription to a Massachusetts pharmacist. Assume a valid electronic-prescribing exception applies and the prescription was issued today. Which actions are required under the Massachusetts out-of-state prescription rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Dispense if authenticity cannot be established but the patient has an insurance card.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute prohibits dispensing if the required verification cannot be obtained.

choices.text: Treat the prescription as Schedule II because it crossed a state line.
choices.why: Incorrect. Origin does not alter the controlled-substance schedule.

choices.text: Verify the prescription by telephone or another appropriate means.
choices.why: Correct. The statute requires verification for interstate Schedule III–V prescriptions.

choices.text: Require a new DEA registration solely because the practitioner lives in Vermont.
choices.why: Incorrect. A practitioner meeting the stated out-of-state requirements need not obtain a separate registration merely to use this pathway.

choices.text: Record that the pharmacist requested the practitioner to send a written prescription within seven days or the shorter applicable federal period.
choices.why: Correct. This is the express requirement for oral interstate Schedule III–V orders.

critical_error_options.reason: The statute prohibits dispensing if the required verification cannot be obtained.

questions.topic: Hospital internal practitioner code verification list
questions.trigger: A DEA-registered hospital authorizes employed practitioners to prescribe controlled substances under its institutional registration. An outside dispensing pharmacy asks the hospital to verify which practitioner is assigned a particular internal suffix. Which requirement applies under federal law?
questions.legal_decision: Hospital keeps a current practitioner/code list and makes it available at all times to other registrants and law enforcement on request.
questions.critical_exception: The hospital's list is not restricted to its own staff or DEA alone.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the practitioner uses an individual DEA registration, this institutional-suffix verification rule does not apply to that prescription.
questions.stem: A DEA-registered hospital authorizes employed practitioners to prescribe controlled substances under its institutional registration. An outside dispensing pharmacy asks the hospital to verify which practitioner is assigned a particular internal suffix. Which requirement applies under federal law?

choices.text: Only the hospital's own pharmacy can request verification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Other registrants may request the list.

choices.text: The hospital may make the list available only during annual inspections.
choices.why: Incorrect. It must be available at all times upon qualifying request.

choices.text: The hospital must maintain the current list and make it available to other registrants and law enforcement upon request.
choices.why: Correct. This permits verification of the practitioner's authority.

choices.text: The hospital should assign one shared suffix to all practitioners.
choices.why: Incorrect. A specific internal code is assigned to each authorized practitioner.

choices.text: The hospital need not retain the list once suffixes are assigned.
choices.why: Incorrect. A current list must be kept.

questions.topic: Individual practitioner's employee DEA exemption does not authorize prescriptions
questions.trigger: A physician employed in another individually DEA-registered physician's private practice has no individual DEA registration. The employee is authorized under state law to administer and dispense controlled substances within the employment and meets the federal employee exemption. The employer is not a mid-level practitioner or institutional registrant. Under 21 CFR 1301.22(b), which action is NOT covered by this exemption?
questions.legal_decision: Issuing controlled-substance prescriptions is excluded from this particular individual-practitioner employee exemption.
questions.critical_exception: Institutional practitioner registration under subsection (c) is a distinct route.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An appropriate individual DEA registration or applicable institutional exemption could change prescribing authority.
questions.stem: A physician employed in another individually DEA-registered physician's private practice has no individual DEA registration. The employee is authorized under state law to administer and dispense controlled substances within the employment and meets the federal employee exemption. The employer is not a mid-level practitioner or institutional registrant. Under 21 CFR 1301.22(b), which action is NOT covered by this exemption?

choices.text: Administering an authorized controlled drug in normal employment.
choices.why: Incorrect. Administration within applicable jurisdictional authority is covered.

choices.text: Dispensing a controlled drug directly, other than by prescription issuance, within the stated authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exemption expressly covers that form of dispensing.

choices.text: Issuing a controlled-substance prescription using the employer's individual DEA registration.
choices.why: Correct. Prescription issuance is specifically excluded from subsection (b).

choices.text: Administering a controlled drug while acting within the employee's authorized practice.
choices.why: Incorrect. That action is within the stated exemption.

choices.text: Directly dispensing under the employer registration within state-authorized limits without writing a prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. This is within the described exemption.

questions.topic: Phendimetrazine versus phentermine scheduling
questions.trigger: A pharmacist receives prescriptions for phendimetrazine and phentermine, each as an ordinary single-ingredient product. Which federal and Massachusetts schedule pair is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Phendimetrazine is Schedule III and phentermine is Schedule IV.
questions.critical_exception: Massachusetts incorporates federal schedules I–V.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Different drugs in the same therapeutic class need not share a schedule.
questions.stem: A pharmacist receives prescriptions for phendimetrazine and phentermine, each as an ordinary single-ingredient product. Which federal and Massachusetts schedule pair is correct?

choices.text: Both are Schedule IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. Phendimetrazine is Schedule III.

choices.text: Both are Schedule VI only.
choices.why: Incorrect. Both are federally scheduled.

choices.text: Both are Schedule II.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither listed drug is Schedule II.

choices.text: Phendimetrazine III; phentermine IV.
choices.why: Correct. Each is listed in the respective schedule.

choices.text: Phendimetrazine IV; phentermine III.
choices.why: Incorrect. The classifications are reversed.

questions.topic: Emergency medication authority when planning vaccination service
questions.trigger: Before a community vaccination clinic opens, the pharmacist confirms a valid vaccine standing order but discovers that neither a prescription nor a standing order authorizes the emergency medications used to manage post-vaccination adverse events. All staff training and other conditions are met. What must the pharmacy arrange under Policy 2023-02 before providing this service?
questions.legal_decision: A prescription or standing order authorizing emergency medications is also required.
questions.critical_exception: A vaccine-only order does not itself satisfy the emergency-medication order requirement.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A compliant standing order covering both vaccination and appropriate emergency treatment could satisfy these order requirements.
questions.stem: Before a community vaccination clinic opens, the pharmacist confirms a valid vaccine standing order but discovers that neither a prescription nor a standing order authorizes the emergency medications used to manage post-vaccination adverse events. All staff training and other conditions are met. What must the pharmacy arrange under Policy 2023-02 before providing this service?

choices.text: No emergency order is needed if all personnel have CPR training.
choices.why: Incorrect. Training does not replace order authority.

choices.text: Arrange a valid prescription or standing order for the emergency medications.
choices.why: Correct. Section IV(B) requires this in addition to vaccine authorization.

choices.text: Replace the vaccine standing order with a technician's oral approval.
choices.why: Incorrect. A technician cannot supply practitioner order authority.

choices.text: Rely solely on manufacturer package inserts as emergency orders.
choices.why: Incorrect. Product labeling is not a prescription or standing order.

choices.text: The vaccine standing order automatically covers every emergency medication.
choices.why: Incorrect. Emergency medication authority is separately required.

critical_error_options.reason: Omits required emergency medication order authority.

questions.topic: Pediatric vaccine communication when free program is not used
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy does not use free pediatric vaccines through the state Immunization Program. A parent brings a 12-year-old for a routine non-influenza, non-COVID childhood immunization. Assume age, order and all clinical requirements are met. Which communications are required by Policy 2023-02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Inform parent of potential costs and free vaccination through primary care; counsel on importance of ongoing pediatric or family-practice relationship.
questions.critical_exception: The childhood counseling provision excludes influenza and COVID visits, but the cost disclosure provision applies when free pediatric vaccines are not used.
questions.counterfactual_flip: For an influenza-only visit the specific childhood relationship counseling requirement in VI(C) would not apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy does not use free pediatric vaccines through the state Immunization Program. A parent brings a 12-year-old for a routine non-influenza, non-COVID childhood immunization. Assume age, order and all clinical requirements are met. Which communications are required by Policy 2023-02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Require the parent to transfer the child's primary care to the pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule promotes an ongoing relationship with a primary care provider, not transfer to the pharmacy.

choices.text: Explain potential costs to the parent.
choices.why: Correct. This is required when the pharmacy does not use the free pediatric vaccine program.

choices.text: Tell the parent that the child's primary care provider can provide vaccines at no charge.
choices.why: Correct. The required cost disclosure includes this information.

choices.text: Omit cost disclosure when the child is insured.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy does not create that exception.

choices.text: Counsel about maintaining a pediatric or family-practice relationship for ongoing care.
choices.why: Correct. This is required for the described childhood vaccination visit.

questions.topic: Patient counseling tailored to relevant missed-dose and monitoring instructions
questions.trigger: A patient accepts counseling for a newly prescribed medication. The pharmacist determines that self-monitoring and what to do after a missed dose are particularly important for safe use. The patient already knows the medication's name and strength. Which approach complies with Massachusetts counseling standards?
questions.legal_decision: Provide counseling using professional judgment about information needed for proper use, including the relevant monitoring and missed-dose actions.
questions.critical_exception: Counseling is individualized rather than limited to reading a label.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a topic is not relevant in the pharmacist's judgment, the illustrative list is not a mandatory identical script for every patient.
questions.stem: A patient accepts counseling for a newly prescribed medication. The pharmacist determines that self-monitoring and what to do after a missed dose are particularly important for safe use. The patient already knows the medication's name and strength. Which approach complies with Massachusetts counseling standards?

choices.text: Provide no counseling because the patient can read the label.
choices.why: Incorrect. The patient accepted counseling for new therapy.

choices.text: Read every possible adverse effect regardless of relevance and omit missed-dose instructions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule calls for clinically relevant information based on professional judgment.

choices.text: Ask a technician to make the independent clinical counseling decisions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Counseling is reserved to pharmacists or pharmacy interns.

choices.text: Only repeat the name and strength because the written label is complete.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacist identified additional information necessary for proper use.

choices.text: Explain the pertinent monitoring and missed-dose instructions as part of individualized counseling.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly includes these topics when relevant to understanding proper use.

critical_error_options.reason: Counseling is reserved to pharmacists or pharmacy interns.

questions.topic: Controlled medication disposal after death of ultimate user
questions.trigger: An adult patient dies while lawfully possessing dispensed Schedule II tablets. The executor is lawfully entitled to dispose of the patient's property and has lawful possession of the tablets. A nearby DEA-authorized collection receptacle accepts this dosage form. Which action is permissible under federal law?
questions.legal_decision: The legally entitled executor may transfer the drug for destruction through an authorized collector in a manner permitted by Part 1317.
questions.critical_exception: This does not permit redispensing or return to active inventory.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An unrelated person with no lawful entitlement or possession cannot rely on the decedent-property authorization.
questions.stem: An adult patient dies while lawfully possessing dispensed Schedule II tablets. The executor is lawfully entitled to dispose of the patient's property and has lawful possession of the tablets. A nearby DEA-authorized collection receptacle accepts this dosage form. Which action is permissible under federal law?

choices.text: The executor may return the tablets to active dispensing inventory.
choices.why: Incorrect. Collection for destruction is not inventory return.

choices.text: Only the deceased patient could ever lawfully dispose of the medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule specifically authorizes a qualifying person entitled to dispose of the decedent's property.

choices.text: The executor may sell the remaining tablets to another patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision permits disposal, not sales.

choices.text: The executor must obtain an individual DEA registration solely to use the collector.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly authorizes qualifying nonregistrants.

choices.text: The executor may use the authorized collection receptacle for disposal.
choices.why: Correct. The decedent-property provision permits this transfer for destruction.

critical_error_options.reason: Returns previously dispensed controlled medication to active stock.

questions.topic: HIPAA oral agreement limited to friend's involvement in care
questions.trigger: A competent adult orally agrees that a friend may hear instructions for today's antibiotic because the friend will help with administration. The friend also asks for the patient's unrelated prescription history. No other disclosure authority applies. What may the pharmacy disclose under the involvement-in-care provision?
questions.legal_decision: Disclose information directly relevant to the friend's involvement with the antibiotic, not unrelated medication history.
questions.critical_exception: Oral agreement can support the limited disclosure without a formal written authorization.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An appropriate separate authorization or other legal basis might permit additional disclosure.
questions.stem: A competent adult orally agrees that a friend may hear instructions for today's antibiotic because the friend will help with administration. The friend also asks for the patient's unrelated prescription history. No other disclosure authority applies. What may the pharmacy disclose under the involvement-in-care provision?

choices.text: Disclose the unrelated history if the friend promises confidentiality.
choices.why: Incorrect. That promise does not supply legal authority.

choices.text: Disclose the entire profile because the patient orally agreed to some information sharing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The permitted scope is directly relevant information.

choices.text: Refuse even the agreed instructions because there is no written HIPAA authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. Oral agreement may suffice for this provision.

choices.text: Disclose only directly relevant antibiotic instructions, withholding unrelated prescription history.
choices.why: Correct. This respects the patient's limited agreement and the friend's role.

choices.text: Disclose every controlled prescription but no other medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. There is no such schedule-based rule.

questions.topic: Schedule V refill limit in Massachusetts despite federal distinction
questions.trigger: An otherwise valid Schedule V prescription issued three months ago has already been refilled five times. The prescriber originally wrote that eight refills were authorized. A patient requests the sixth refill. Which response complies with Massachusetts law?
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense the sixth refill under this prescription; obtain a new valid prescription if appropriate.
questions.critical_exception: Massachusetts limits Schedule V prescriptions to five refills as well as six months; remaining time is not enough.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If fewer than five refills had occurred and other conditions were satisfied, a refill could be permitted.
questions.stem: An otherwise valid Schedule V prescription issued three months ago has already been refilled five times. The prescriber originally wrote that eight refills were authorized. A patient requests the sixth refill. Which response complies with Massachusetts law?

choices.text: Decline the sixth refill under this prescription; obtain a new valid prescription if appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Five refills is the state maximum.

choices.text: Treat the sixth refill as the original fill.
choices.why: Incorrect. A completed original dispensing cannot be relabeled.

choices.text: Apply only the Schedule VI one-year rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. Schedule V is subject to its own rule.

choices.text: Refill because fewer than six months have passed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The five-refill limit also applies.

choices.text: Refill because the prescriber authorized eight refills.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescriber authorization cannot override the legal ceiling.

critical_error_options.reason: Dispenses beyond the Massachusetts Schedule V refill limit.

questions.topic: Positive identification of the person collecting a controlled prescription
questions.trigger: A patient's adult agent comes to collect the patient's Schedule III prescription. The agent shows the patient's valid government-issued identification but not the agent's own identification. No serious hardship or Commissioner waiver applies. Which actions follow the Massachusetts positive identification rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Inspect the identification of the agent actually receiving the prescription; patient ID alone does not satisfy the rule in this scenario.
questions.critical_exception: The ultimate user or the agent to whom the drug is dispensed must present the applicable customer identifier.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the patient personally received the drug, the patient's own qualifying identification could satisfy the rule.
questions.stem: A patient's adult agent comes to collect the patient's Schedule III prescription. The agent shows the patient's valid government-issued identification but not the agent's own identification. No serious hardship or Commissioner waiver applies. Which actions follow the Massachusetts positive identification rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Release using only the absent patient's identification.
choices.why: Incorrect. That is not the agent's identification.

choices.text: Withhold release unless the identification requirement or an applicable exception is satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. No exception is established in the facts.

choices.text: Substitute the pharmacy technician's identification number.
choices.why: Incorrect. The technician is not the receiving ultimate user or agent.

choices.text: Assume every agent automatically qualifies for hardship.
choices.why: Incorrect. Hardship requires a factual reason and prescribed documentation.

choices.text: Ask the agent to present the agent's qualifying government-issued identification.
choices.why: Correct. The customer identifier relates to the person receiving the drug.

critical_error_options.reason: Releases despite unmet positive identification requirement.

questions.topic: Initial EPCS transfer corrupted by intermediary conversion
questions.trigger: At the patient's request, a retail pharmacy attempts a first transfer of an unfilled original electronic Schedule III prescription to a Massachusetts retail pharmacy. The intermediary converts it to a fax and truncates the prescriber's address. The receiver can independently locate the address. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense from the altered/converted transfer; authorized initial EPCS transfer must remain electronic with required contents intact.
questions.critical_exception: The one-time patient-requested transfer authority does not permit conversion or alteration.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If transmitted electronically without alteration, directly between pharmacists with required documentation and other conditions met, a first transfer could be lawful.
questions.stem: At the patient's request, a retail pharmacy attempts a first transfer of an unfilled original electronic Schedule III prescription to a Massachusetts retail pharmacy. The intermediary converts it to a fax and truncates the prescriber's address. The receiver can independently locate the address. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: All remaining refills can be dispensed from the corrupted transfer because it is Schedule III.
choices.why: Incorrect. Refill authority does not cure the invalid initial transfer.

choices.text: The conversion to fax violates the initial electronic transfer requirements.
choices.why: Correct. The prescription must remain in electronic form during transfer.

choices.text: The receiving pharmacist may dispense after typing the missing address into the fax record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Alteration of required contents invalidates the transfer; manual repair does not cure it.

choices.text: The truncation is independently a reason the transferred prescription is invalid.
choices.why: Correct. The federal rule expressly prohibits alteration or truncation.

choices.text: A patient request waives the electronic-form requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient request is a prerequisite, not a waiver.

critical_error_options.reason: Alteration of required contents invalidates the transfer; manual repair does not cure it.

questions.topic: Documenting DUR intervention after direct patient consultation
questions.trigger: Before dispensing a new prescription, a pharmacist identifies a drug-allergy alert. Direct consultation with the patient and review of reliable records establish that the recorded allergy was entered for the wrong patient. After correcting the record, the pharmacist determines dispensing is appropriate. Which actions are consistent with 247 CMR 9.17? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Use appropriate professional measures, including patient consultation when appropriate, and document measures taken in response to DUR.
questions.critical_exception: Resolving an alert does not eliminate the requirement to document the intervention.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the allergy concern remained unresolved, further appropriate measures would be needed.
questions.stem: Before dispensing a new prescription, a pharmacist identifies a drug-allergy alert. Direct consultation with the patient and review of reliable records establish that the recorded allergy was entered for the wrong patient. After correcting the record, the pharmacist determines dispensing is appropriate. Which actions are consistent with 247 CMR 9.17? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Use direct consultation with the patient as an appropriate measure when it resolves the concern.
choices.why: Correct. Patient or agent consultation is one of the permitted measures.

choices.text: Let an automated alert override serve as the entire clinical review without pharmacist assessment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The duty requires pharmacist professional review and appropriate measures.

choices.text: Treat every alert as an absolute permanent prohibition on dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule requires appropriate measures, not automatic permanent refusal.

choices.text: Document the measures taken to resolve the DUR finding.
choices.why: Correct. The rule expressly requires documentation.

choices.text: Omit documentation because the finding was resolved.
choices.why: Incorrect. Documentation applies to measures taken, not only unresolved alerts.

questions.topic: PMP reporting for lawful nonresident delivery into Massachusetts
questions.trigger: A pharmacy located in another state is appropriately licensed to ship prescriptions to Massachusetts. It delivers a reportable Schedule III prescription to a person in Massachusetts. It does not have a physical Massachusetts store. No reporting waiver or other exception applies. Which statement is correct?
questions.legal_decision: The nonresident pharmacy delivering a reportable controlled substance into Massachusetts is subject to Massachusetts PMP reporting.
questions.critical_exception: The reporting obligation is based on qualifying delivery into Massachusetts as well as resident dispensing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A transaction without delivery into Massachusetts would not trigger this particular interstate reporting provision.
questions.stem: A pharmacy located in another state is appropriately licensed to ship prescriptions to Massachusetts. It delivers a reportable Schedule III prescription to a person in Massachusetts. It does not have a physical Massachusetts store. No reporting waiver or other exception applies. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: No Massachusetts reporting because the pharmacy is physically out of state.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule explicitly includes interstate delivery to a person in Massachusetts.

choices.text: Only Schedule II interstate deliveries are reportable.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule covers Schedules II–V and designated additional drugs.

choices.text: The patient's residence makes reporting optional.
choices.why: Incorrect. Qualifying delivery into Massachusetts triggers the requirement.

choices.text: The pharmacy must transmit required dispensing information under the Massachusetts PMP rules.
choices.why: Correct. It is included in the reporting class.

choices.text: Only the prescriber submits the pharmacy's dispensing report.
choices.why: Incorrect. The dispensing pharmacy has the reporting obligation.

questions.topic: Authorized person requesting Schedule II partial fill
questions.trigger: A competent adult has a valid Schedule II prescription for 30 tablets. A friend authorized only to pick up prescriptions asks the pharmacist to dispense 10 tablets instead, without a request from the patient or prescriber. The friend is not named in a medical power of attorney. There is sufficient stock, and no other partial-fill exception applies. Under the federal patient-requested rule, which response is correct?
questions.legal_decision: The friend's pickup authorization alone does not qualify the friend to request a partial fill; obtain a request from an authorized person.
questions.critical_exception: Adult caregiver must be named in a medical power of attorney to qualify under this route.
questions.counterfactual_flip: The adult patient can request a partial fill directly, subject to state and federal conditions.
questions.stem: A competent adult has a valid Schedule II prescription for 30 tablets. A friend authorized only to pick up prescriptions asks the pharmacist to dispense 10 tablets instead, without a request from the patient or prescriber. The friend is not named in a medical power of attorney. There is sufficient stock, and no other partial-fill exception applies. Under the federal patient-requested rule, which response is correct?

choices.text: Convert the remaining quantity into a refill.
choices.why: Incorrect. Schedule II prescriptions cannot be refilled.

choices.text: Honor the friend's request because anyone permitted to pick up may request partial filling.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pickup authority is not the specified medical power of attorney.

choices.text: Honor the request as a stock-shortage partial fill.
choices.why: Incorrect. Sufficient stock is available.

choices.text: Obtain a qualifying request from the patient, prescribing practitioner, or an authorized representative under the federal rule.
choices.why: Correct. The stated friend's request alone is insufficient.

choices.text: Require a medical power of attorney even if the patient makes the request personally.
choices.why: Incorrect. The patient may personally request it.

questions.topic: Prescriber-specific conventional package request does not carry to another prescription
questions.trigger: A physician directs use of an easy-open container for one oral prescription subject to child-resistant packaging. The patient later presents a different prescription from the same physician with no such direction. The patient has never requested conventional packaging for all medicines. Both drugs are otherwise subject to special packaging. Which response complies with the PPPA?
questions.legal_decision: Use special packaging for the separate prescription unless a valid new prescriber direction or purchaser request applies.
questions.critical_exception: A prescriber direction for one prescription is not a blanket waiver for other prescriptions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A specific patient request applying to all prescriptions could support conventional packaging for the later prescription.
questions.stem: A physician directs use of an easy-open container for one oral prescription subject to child-resistant packaging. The patient later presents a different prescription from the same physician with no such direction. The patient has never requested conventional packaging for all medicines. Both drugs are otherwise subject to special packaging. Which response complies with the PPPA?

choices.text: Use conventional packaging because the drugs are prescribed by the same person.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prescriber's identity does not extend the prior direction.

choices.text: Ask the cashier to decide whether the patient probably prefers easy-open packaging.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception depends on the purchaser's request or prescriber's direction, not staff inference.

choices.text: Never use conventional packaging even if the patient specifically requests it.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute permits the purchaser's specific request.

choices.text: Use an easy-open container for all future prescriptions from that physician.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prescription-specific direction does not carry over to different prescriptions.

choices.text: Use child-resistant packaging for the new prescription unless an applicable request or direction is obtained.
choices.why: Correct. Neither a qualifying new direction nor a blanket patient request is present.

questions.citation: 15 USC 1473(b); CPSC Poison Prevention Packaging Guide, Part 3

critical_error_options.reason: A prescription-specific direction does not carry over to different prescriptions.

questions.topic: Expired manufacturer stock cannot be dispensed to patient
questions.trigger: While checking a prescription, the pharmacist finds that the manufacturer's expiration date on the stock bottle passed last month. The patient urgently needs the medicine but is not legally authorized to receive expired stock. Which action is permitted?
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense expired stock to the patient; seek an appropriate unexpired supply.
questions.critical_exception: The rule distinguishes ordinary patient dispensing from transfer to an entity legally authorized to receive such products.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the product were in date and otherwise suitable, expiry would no longer prohibit dispensing.
questions.stem: While checking a prescription, the pharmacist finds that the manufacturer's expiration date on the stock bottle passed last month. The patient urgently needs the medicine but is not legally authorized to receive expired stock. Which action is permitted?

choices.text: Dispense the expired medicine with a verbal warning.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient notification does not override the prohibition.

choices.text: Dispense it if the manufacturer bottle is unopened.
choices.why: Incorrect. An intact bottle does not erase the expiration date.

choices.text: Dispense it after the patient signs consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Consent does not authorize ordinary dispensing of expired stock.

choices.text: Change the expiration date to the date of dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. A pharmacist cannot extend the manufacturer's expiry by relabeling.

choices.text: Do not dispense the expired drug and seek suitable stock.
choices.why: Correct. Ordinary patient dispensing of an expired product is prohibited.

critical_error_options.reason: Patient notification does not override the prohibition.

questions.topic: DEA Form 222 unexecuted forms kept at another location
questions.trigger: A registered pharmacy keeps blank, unexecuted paper DEA Forms 222 in its chain's administrative office rather than at the registered pharmacy address. What condition must be met under the federal rule governing this arrangement?
questions.legal_decision: Unexecuted forms may be kept or executed away from the printed registered location if promptly delivered to that location upon an authorized inspection.
questions.critical_exception: This permission concerns unexecuted forms, not a blanket offsite-record exemption.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If forms cannot be delivered promptly when an authorized inspection occurs, the stated offsite arrangement is not compliant.
questions.stem: A registered pharmacy keeps blank, unexecuted paper DEA Forms 222 in its chain's administrative office rather than at the registered pharmacy address. What condition must be met under the federal rule governing this arrangement?

choices.text: Ensure prompt delivery of all unexecuted forms to the registered location upon an authorized inspection.
choices.why: Correct. This is the explicit condition for offsite retention or execution.

choices.text: Destroy the forms every time an inspector requests them.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires availability, not destruction.

choices.text: Blank forms must always be stored at the printed registered address with no exception.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal rule expressly permits another location under a condition.

choices.text: An administrative office may permanently refuse access to the forms.
choices.why: Incorrect. The forms must be delivered promptly upon inspection.

choices.text: Only a wholesaler may keep blank forms away from its registered address.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision is not limited to wholesalers.

questions.topic: Red C exception requires all specified electronic retrieval capabilities
questions.trigger: A pharmacy files Schedule III–V paper prescriptions with its noncontrolled paper prescriptions. Its computer application identifies prescriptions by number and retrieves originals by patient, drug and date filled, but cannot retrieve them by prescriber name. The pharmacy wants to omit the red C marking. Which statement follows the federal rule?
questions.legal_decision: The electronic-system waiver is not established; use compliant separate filing or meet the readily retrievable red C requirements.
questions.critical_exception: The waiver requires identification by prescription number and retrieval by all four specified fields.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Adding prescriber-name retrieval would meet the described missing element.
questions.stem: A pharmacy files Schedule III–V paper prescriptions with its noncontrolled paper prescriptions. Its computer application identifies prescriptions by number and retrieves originals by patient, drug and date filled, but cannot retrieve them by prescriber name. The pharmacy wants to omit the red C marking. Which statement follows the federal rule?

choices.text: Correct the system to permit prescriber-name retrieval or use an otherwise compliant filing method.
choices.why: Correct. The missing retrieval capability prevents the described waiver.

choices.text: Use a half-inch blue C instead.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated marking standard is a red C at least one inch high in the lower right corner.

choices.text: Discard original paper prescriptions once data are indexed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The waiver is for the marking, not retention of originals.

choices.text: Omit the mark because three retrieval fields are enough.
choices.why: Incorrect. All listed retrieval capabilities are required for the waiver.

choices.text: Omit the mark because Schedule III–V prescriptions may never require it.
choices.why: Incorrect. The mixed-file method has marking requirements unless waived.

questions.topic: Required policies for controlled medication delivery by common carrier
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy starts mailing controlled prescriptions through an independent common carrier. The carrier has general parcel procedures, but the pharmacy has no policies or procedures for packing, shipping, transporting or delivering controlled substances. Which action is required?
questions.legal_decision: Maintain pharmacy policies and procedures addressing packing, shipping, transportation and delivery of controlled substances.
questions.critical_exception: Using an outside carrier does not remove the pharmacy's obligation.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A pharmacy with appropriate policies that address these processes would satisfy this specific requirement.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy starts mailing controlled prescriptions through an independent common carrier. The carrier has general parcel procedures, but the pharmacy has no policies or procedures for packing, shipping, transporting or delivering controlled substances. Which action is required?

choices.text: Rely exclusively on the carrier's general parcel procedures without pharmacy procedures.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacy must maintain its own applicable policies and procedures.

choices.text: Maintain policies only for packing, not transport or delivery.
choices.why: Incorrect. All four processes are specified.

choices.text: Maintain pharmacy policies and procedures covering packing, shipping, transporting and delivering controlled substances.
choices.why: Correct. This is the express requirement.

choices.text: Prohibit all mailing of controlled drugs solely because they are controlled.
choices.why: Incorrect. Mail or common-carrier dispensing is allowed when consistent with other laws.

choices.text: Create delivery procedures only after a loss occurs.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule is not triggered only after a loss.

questions.topic: Interoperable electronic prescribing technology and biologic substitution
questions.trigger: A pharmacist lawfully substitutes an FDA-interchangeable biologic for a brand-name biological prescription. The pharmacist uses interoperable electronic prescribing technology and can enter the substitution into the patient's interoperable electronic health record. Which notification actions are required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Enter substitution into the patient's EHR within a reasonable time for prescriber notice; provide written notice to patient or authorized representative.
questions.critical_exception: Alternative notification methods apply if the pharmacist lacks ability to make the EHR notation.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If EHR notation were unavailable, an authorized alternative prescriber-notification route would be permitted.
questions.stem: A pharmacist lawfully substitutes an FDA-interchangeable biologic for a brand-name biological prescription. The pharmacist uses interoperable electronic prescribing technology and can enter the substitution into the patient's interoperable electronic health record. Which notification actions are required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Give only verbal patient notice because EHR entry is completed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Written patient notification is still required.

choices.text: Omit both notifications because FDA determined interchangeability.
choices.why: Incorrect. FDA interchangeability does not remove state notification duties.

choices.text: Notify the prescriber by recording the substitution in the interoperable EHR.
choices.why: Correct. This is required in the stated circumstances.

choices.text: Use only fax instead of the available interoperable EHR entry.
choices.why: Incorrect. The alternative route is for inability to make the EHR notation.

choices.text: Provide written notification to the patient or authorized representative.
choices.why: Correct. Patient notification is a separate written-notice requirement.

questions.topic: Compounding a product withdrawn for safety or effectiveness
questions.trigger: A pharmacy operating under section 503A receives a patient-specific prescription for a drug product expressly listed in 21 CFR 216.24 as withdrawn from the market for safety or effectiveness. The practitioner states that the patient prefers this product. Which action is consistent with federal compounding law?
questions.legal_decision: Do not compound that listed drug product under section 503A.
questions.critical_exception: A patient-specific prescription or preference does not override the withdrawn-product restriction.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A different product not on the list would still require compliance with all applicable compounding conditions.
questions.stem: A pharmacy operating under section 503A receives a patient-specific prescription for a drug product expressly listed in 21 CFR 216.24 as withdrawn from the market for safety or effectiveness. The practitioner states that the patient prefers this product. Which action is consistent with federal compounding law?

choices.text: Compound it if the patient signs a waiver.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient consent does not establish the statutory exemption.

choices.text: Do not compound the listed product under section 503A.
choices.why: Correct. The statutory condition and implementing list expressly exclude it.

choices.text: Compound it in a smaller batch to avoid the restriction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Batch size does not remove the listed-product restriction.

choices.text: Compound it if the patient pays without insurance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payment method does not change federal eligibility.

choices.text: Compound it because a patient-specific prescription always overrides the list.
choices.why: Incorrect. The withdrawal restriction remains applicable.

critical_error_options.reason: Compounds a product explicitly excluded from the 503A exemption.

questions.topic: Board suitability discretion regarding pharmacy interest holder
questions.trigger: A company applies for a Massachusetts drug store pharmacy license. An interest holder previously held an ownership interest in another pharmacy whose license was revoked in disciplinary proceedings. The company argues that because this is a new legal entity, the Board cannot consider the prior history. Which conclusion follows?
questions.legal_decision: The Board may consider the interest holder's prior ownership of a disciplined pharmacy when deciding suitability; the result is discretionary.
questions.critical_exception: The provision authorizes consideration rather than imposing automatic denial solely on this fact.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If there were no such prior interest or adverse history, this particular suitability factor would not be established.
questions.stem: A company applies for a Massachusetts drug store pharmacy license. An interest holder previously held an ownership interest in another pharmacy whose license was revoked in disciplinary proceedings. The company argues that because this is a new legal entity, the Board cannot consider the prior history. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: The Board must ignore the history because the applicant is a new entity.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly includes an interest holder's history.

choices.text: The application must automatically be denied under all circumstances.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation gives the Board discretion.

choices.text: The Board may consider the prior history in determining suitability.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection (4) identifies this factor.

choices.text: Only the proposed manager's personal license is relevant.
choices.why: Incorrect. The suitability rule includes applicants, licensees and interest holders.

choices.text: The company may omit the history whenever a new EIN is obtained.
choices.why: Incorrect. A new entity does not eliminate the suitability factor.
